title: The Drowned Log

pages.text:
*The Gatekeeper's Rules, Rule 23: A hard problem is usually three easy problems standing close together.*

Shu wiped the chalk dust from her knees, her trousers dark with rain and mud, and looked at the diagram one last time. The lines were clean, the angles sharp. It was not a picture of a jammed gate; it was a list of three small failures that had conspired to make one large one. The water was pressing too hard. The log was wedged too tight. The lever had no room to swing. She stood up, her joints popping in the cold, and pointed to the first line on her wet paper.

"First," she said, her voice steady despite the hammering of the storm against the stone arch. "We cannot pull against the water. The hydrostatic pressure on that bronze frame is now equivalent to a small car parked on it. If we pull, the pin will shear, or the wood will split. We must relieve the head." She pointed to the Moon Basin, dark and swollen behind the island’s green rim. "We build a siphon. From the high water to the channel. We drain a little, just enough to drop the pressure by half a meter. The water will do the work of unloading the gate."

Han, who was shivering in his orange life vest, looked at the island wall, then at Shu. "Over the wall?"

"Over the wall," Shu confirmed. "A hose is too thin. We need a pipe, or a chain of buckets if we are desperate. But we need volume. Ouyang." She turned to the engineer, who was hunching over her waterproof plans, her silver glasses fogged. "Do you have a pump, or at least a flexible pipe? Something that can move water faster than a human arm can?"

Ouyang looked up, wiping her eyes with the back of a gloved hand. She nodded slowly, a professional calculation already moving behind her gaze. "I have a heavy-duty irrigation line in the camp. It is rated for pressure. It will not break. But it needs a prime. It needs the suction started."

"Then we start it," said Shu. "And then we float the log." She drew a second circle in the chalk. "Empty drums. Oil drums. We lash them to the log, turning it into a pontoon. If it is buoyant, it will lift off the silt bed. It will stop biting into the channel floor."

"And the third?" asked Uncle Liu, who had appeared in the shadows, his leather apron steaming in the cool air.

Shu drew the final line, a long diagonal across the channel. "We pull it out. But not with muscles. We use the temple pillars. Block and tackle. Eight strands. A mechanical advantage of eight to one. We do not pull the log. We pull a rope, and the rope pulls the log, and the log moves because the geometry says it must." She looked around the group, at the rain and the dark water and the frightened faces. "Three easy problems. One hard one. We solve them in order. Who has the drums?"
pages.image: Rain-soaked night scene at stone Dragon Gates, Shu in indigo jacket pointing at chalk diagram on wet rock, Ouyang Min in yellow hard hat holding plans, Uncle Liu in leather apron watching, dark water churning behind them.

pages.text:
The fishermen of Mistwater Landing did not argue. They had been born on that pier, and they knew that when the water rose, the only language that mattered was the language of hands and rope. Within ten minutes, a dozen men were wading through the slush of the dock, carrying the heavy, dented oil drums from the storage shed. They moved with the efficient, silent grace of men who have done this a hundred times, the drums clanking a dull, metallic rhythm against the wet stone.

Han and Uncle Liu were already in the water, their boots submerged to the shin, the cold biting into their skin. Han was lashing the drums to the submerged log with thick hemp rope, his movements fast and practiced. Uncle Liu held the log steady with a pry bar, his muscles straining against the mass of the timber. The log was huge, a dark shape of rotted wood and silt, wedged broadside in the channel like a tooth stuck in a jaw.

"Ouyang, call it!" Shu shouted over the rain. She was on the bank, directing the siphon line. Ouyang stood on the low wall, her voice clear and commanding. "Prime the line! Fill the pipe! Now!"

A-Bao, in his bright yellow raincoat, was running up and down the dock, passing buckets of water from one end to the other, a human chain of liquid. The siphon hissed, a high-pitched whine that grew in volume. Then, with a sudden, violent gurgle, the line snapped taut. A rope of water, thick as a man’s arm, arced over the island wall and plunged into the channel.

The sound was unmistakable. It was not a splash; it was a sigh. The water in the channel dropped, visibly, the black surface falling away from the stone rim. The pressure on the gate eased. The bronze frame, which had been groaning under the strain of the moon, settled.

"Did it work?" Han called out, his face pale with cold and exertion.

"Look at the gauge," Shu said. She pointed to the needle, which had dropped from the red line to the yellow zone. "The head is down by half a meter. The log is no longer fighting the water. Now we pull."

The drums, now floating, bobbed gently around the log. The silt bed, disturbed by the change in pressure, released its grip. The log shifted, a small, grinding movement that sent a spray of muddy water over Uncle Liu’s boots.

"It's moving," Uncle Liu said, his voice thick with surprise. "By itself."

"No," Shu said, her eyes fixed on the gate. "It's ready. Now we give it a push."
pages.image: Nighttime dock scene, Han in orange vest and Uncle Liu in leather apron lashing oil drums to submerged log in dark water, A-Bao in yellow raincoat passing buckets, Ouyang on wall directing, rain falling heavily.

pages.text:
The block and tackle was a thing of beautiful, brutal simplicity. Eight strands of hemp rope, thick as a snake, ran from the anchor point on the temple’s stone pillar, down to the log, and back up. The mechanical advantage was eight to one. For every meter of rope Shu pulled, the log moved only twelve centimeters, but the force multiplied. What one person could not do, eight people could do, provided they pulled together, provided they pulled at the same time.

The village lined up on the rope, not a line but a wave. Aunt Meng stood there, her hair net askew, her red apron tied tight. The fishermen stood shoulder to shoulder, their boots finding purchase on the wet stone. At the very end, A-Bao gripped the rope with small hands, his face set in a mask of determination.

"Heave!" Shu called out.

They pulled. The rope creaked, a sound like a bowstring under tension, while the log groaned with a deep, resonant vibration that seemed to rise from the earth itself. It did not move.

"Again!" Shu shouted. "Together! On the count of three! One, two, three, heave!"

Granny Hua, who had been sitting on a dry rock with a cup of tea, stood up. She did not pull. She beat time with her carved walking stick, tapping the stone with a steady, rhythmic clack. *Clack. Clack. Clack.* It was the beat of the village, the heartbeat of the landing.

They pulled again. The rope stretched until it was taut as a wire, and the log shifted, an inch, then two. The silt gave way. The drums bobbed, the water lapping against them. The log slid, grinding against the stone floor of the channel, a sound like a giant clearing its throat.

"Keep pulling!" Shu yelled, her voice raw. "Do not let go! The momentum is your friend! Let it carry you!"

The log began to move with them, the water flowing around them rather than fighting. The rope sang a high, thin note of triumph. The village leaned, their bodies a single unit, their breath a single exhalation. The log slid, faster now, the drums bobbing, the water churning.

"Clear!" Uncle Liu shouted. "It's clear!"

The rope went slack. The log was free.
pages.image: Group of villagers including Aunt Meng and A-Bao in yellow raincoat pulling thick rope in tug-of-war stance on wet stone, Granny Hua beating time with stick, Shu directing, rain and mist around them.

pages.text:
The log shot out of the channel with a speed that surprised them all. It did not slide; it flew. The water, released from its confinement, rushed in to fill the void, pushing the buoyant drums ahead. The log hit the net of the Magpie, the ferry that was waiting just beyond the gate, with a splash that drenched Ouyang from head to toe.

She sputtered, her white shirt soaked through, her glasses sliding down her nose. "I am going to need a new shirt," she said, shaking her hair, a strand of black clinging to her forehead. "And I am billing you all for it."

Uncle Liu was already at the lever. He gripped the bronze handle, the cold metal biting into his palms. He did not pull. He waited. He felt the vibration of the water, the long, slow sigh of the basin as it settled. Then, with a steady, deliberate motion, he pulled.

The gate lurching upward was a small, precise movement. But it was enough. The Moon Dragon, the carved stone head with its bronze eyes, opened by a whole step. The water, held back for thirty years, began to flow. It was not a surge; it was a stream. A steady, continuous flow, moving from the Moon Basin into the Sun Basin, sharing the weight, balancing the level.

The Moon Basin gave a long, slow, grateful sigh. The water level dropped, just a fraction, but it was a drop that meant the difference between a flood and a lake. The low bank above Mistwater Landing was no longer threatened. The pressure was gone. The balance was restored.

Shu leaned against the lever, her legs trembling. She looked at the gate, at the water flowing through it, at the faces of the people around her. They were wet, they were tired, they were alive.

"We did it," Han said, his voice quiet.

"No," Shu said. "We started it. There are more steps."
pages.image: Night scene, huge log caught in ferry net with splash, Ouyang Min soaked in white shirt and yellow hard hat, Uncle Liu operating bronze lever, water flowing steadily through opened stone gate, moonlight on water.

pages.text:
The tremor started in Shu’s fingers. It was a fine, irritating vibration that had been masked by the effort of the machinery. Now that the gate stood still, the cold of the bronze lever bit through her wet gloves. The shaking climbed up her wrists and settled in her shoulders, as stubborn as a knot in a bamboo joint. It was the physical echo of thirty minutes spent pushing against a wall that had turned out to be a door. The door had swung open onto a wind she had not expected.

Han saw it. He did not comment on it. He simply shifted his weight closer, his boots sliding slightly on the wet stone. He placed his hand over hers on the cold metal of the lever socket. His palm was warm and dry, a small, solid block of heat against the chill of the bronze. He did not squeeze. He just held, his fingers long and steady. The trembling in her arms began to lose its argument. The rain continued to fall in sheets, drumming a dull rhythm on the stone channel. In the small circle of their joined hands, the world was quiet and fixed.

A-gong was sitting on the wet rock nearby. His straw hat hung limp on the end of his cane. His white beard was dark with rain, dripping onto the stone. He was laughing. It was a wet, broken sound, a low rumble that seemed to come from the bottom of his lungs, from a place that had been dry and dusty for thirty years. He was crying too, the tears mixing with the rain on his face. He did not wipe them away. He just sat there, leaning on his cane, looking at the water flowing through the gate with an expression of bewildered relief.

"Again," he said, his voice thick and rough, barely audible over the rain. "Again, from step five."

Shu looked at him, then at the gate. The water was now flowing in a steady, measured stream, no longer a surge but a current. She straightened her back, feeling the stiffness in her spine. She wiped her hands on her khaki trousers, leaving dark streaks of mud on the fabric. She looked at Han, and he smiled, a small, tired smile. Then he let go of her hand.

"Step five," she said.

The night went on. The rain kept falling. The water found its level, inch by careful inch. And they, together, found their way forward.
